faqs.q: What is digging the small sand mounds in my Fernandina Beach yard?
faqs.a: That depends on the shape. Eastern moles leave raised surface tunnels and small molehills, armadillos leave scattered digging in beds and lawn edges, and in sandy north and central Florida soils a southeastern pocket gopher leaves a row of sand mounds. A large burrow with a wide, half-moon apron of sand is different — that is likely a gopher tortoise burrow, which is protected, carries a 25-foot permit buffer, and must be left alone. Call us and describe the digging and we will identify it before any work is planned.

faqs.q: We just moved to Yulee from up north — which yard animals should we know about?
faqs.a: Three, in order of frequency. Armadillos dig cone-shaped holes at night hunting grubs — lawful to trap, and common. Gopher tortoises dig one large half-moon burrow and are protected — admire and leave alone. And near the creeks, cottonmouths are the one venomous regular to respect, alongside harmless watersnakes and racers. Add roof rats testing new rooflines and you have the Yulee welcome package; our inspection sorts what your lot actually hosts and what, if anything, needs a trap versus a seal versus a smile.

faqs.q: What do I do about Muscovy ducks around my Callahan home?
faqs.a: Feral Muscovy ducks are handled under the federal Control Order: a landowner, or our crew with the landowner's permission, may control them on the property without a federal or state permit, but captured Muscovy ducks may never be released elsewhere — relocation is illegal for this species. Traps are checked at least every 24 hours and any non-target bird is released on site. We will explain the lawful options for your property before any work starts.

faqs.q: Why are roof rats such a problem in Hilliard?
faqs.a: Roof rats are Florida's main structure rat, and Hilliard gives them exactly what they want: palm crowns, fruit trees, dense shrubs, and rooflines they can reach from fences and branches. They nest in attics and wall voids and breed year-round here. Our crew traps and excludes — sealing the entry and cutting back roof access — and frames structure work as nonchemical trapping and exclusion, because chemical rodent work in a structure is FDACS Chapter 482 pest-control territory.

faqs.q: What makes the big sand mounds in our Ratliff field?
faqs.a: Most likely southeastern pocket gophers — solitary burrowing rodents that push fan-shaped mounds of sand as they tunnel after roots and bulbs. They are not moles, whose tunnels ridge the surface, and not gopher tortoises, whose single burrow is a large half-moon and protected. Pocket gophers are lawful trapping work, quoted by the scope of the infestation after we walk the mound field — in open Ratliff ground, a fresh mound line tells us the system's size before a single trap is set.

Nassau Village-Ratliff.wildlife_intro:
Nassau Village-Ratliff is a small rural community in Nassau County's interior — country roads, acreage homes, and pine and farm country between Callahan and the St. Marys River. The wildlife is unhurried and rural: raccoons in the outbuildings, opossums under porches, armadillos and pocket gophers in the fields and yards, deer and turkey daily, and snakes along the creek bottoms. Residents call when an animal moves into a building, and not before.

Our Ratliff service matches that ethic: house-and-barn inspections, coop and feed hardening, porch skirting, and burrow identification, with trapping only where an animal has actually taken up residence. The pocket gopher versus mole versus tortoise lesson is delivered at the yard, in the sand, because out here the education is half the service. Written quotes, daily trap checks, and releases on your land or in-county under the permission rule.
